newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Water seen as potential conflict in SADC region.
newsitem.headline: Water seen as potential conflict in SADC region.

text.p: A senior Southern African Development Community official cautioned on Wednesday that water could trigger conflict in the region unless it was equitably shared and properly utilised.

At a water conference in Lesotho attended by over 100 delegates from 11 of the 12 SADC countries, the SADC's deputy executive secretary, Lengolo Monyake, said water had gained an increasingly important role in the region.
"It is perhaps worth underscoring the fact that water scarcity and the concomitant reliance on shared rivers can be a potential source of conflict at various levels," he said.

"Water scarcity, and the increasing reliance upon shared waters, are increasingly becoming the pivotal issues that will determine the success or failure of the new SADC vision aimed at increasing investment, trade, peace and security and the social and economic development of the region as a whole."

SADC, which groups Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe, represents 40 percent of Africa's population and 80 percent of the continent's GDP.
Studies have indicated that within the next 10 to 30 years Lesotho, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Mauritius will join Malawi, South Africa and Namibia as countries where water is very scarce.
By 2000 over half of southern Africa's population will live in urban areas, further increasing the demand for clean water, according to reports presented to the conference.

Civil strife in Angola, Mozambique, Namibia and South Africa has caused the mass movement of millions of people to urban centres. It has also meant that water resources have not been properly developed.
Angola has only developed about four percent of its existing water resources because of its 20-year-long civil war.
The Zambezi River, which along with its tributaries is vital to some 26 million people in eight countries, generates about 4,500 megawatts (MW) of hydro-electricity out of a potential 20,000.
A report by the Desert Research Foundation of Namibia said at least four future hydro-electric development possibilities for the Zambezi River basin could generate a further 4,500 MW.

The report said more than 50,000 hectares of land could also be brought under irrigation in the next 30 years in the basin which already has over 30 large dams serving industries, mining, irrigation and domestic users.
